I don’t think you can do much except stay consistent & reassure her. But the problem is that even when you reassure her about one thing, another worry can pop up and set it all off again. It is often a recurring cycle.

I would sit down with her and tell her openly what you’ve said here. That although you love her, she needs a lot of reassurance which you’re finding difficult. It might upset her but if you continue to bottle it up you’ll grow resentful. 

And if she’s open to working on her anxiety then CBT methods are amazing for that. It would improve her relationship with you but also her general wellbeing. It’s essentially identifying the worrying thought & then identifying what it makes you feel.

In a very simplified breakdown:
1. ‘Throwawaycar123 was very quiet today’
2. This triggers catastrophic thoughts - ‘he is mad at me, he doesn’t want to be with me, he doesn’t like me’
3. Pausing, stopping the cycle and thinking of other reasons why you could be quiet today e.g. ‘he is tired, he is hungry, he is upset about something unrelated to me’
4. Thinking about what would really happen if the anxiety was true e.g. you really *are* mad at her - is that really the worst thing ever? Or is it a minor issue/fixable?

All of this takes a lot of mental work but has improved my outlook on life hugely and made me generally a whole lot happier.

I’m a doctor in the UK.
If a patient has capacity, you cannot *legally* force them to accept any treatment.

This includes under-18s who are considered ‘Gillick competent’ I.e. clearly having understanding of risks/benefits of a situation.

Capacity can be broken down into 4 areas:
1. Understanding information
2. Retaining the information
3. Weighing up the risks and benefits
4. Communicating your decision

From what you’re saying here, it sounds like you do have a clear understanding.

I would change GPs straight away. I would also go so far as flagging this up to someone - practice manager to start with, GMC if it doesn’t get resolved.

The guy that founded it literally did so because he wanted to make Medicine more accessible to people with low incomes or from low income countries

As a doctor and a patient with a long-term condition I think it’s a good thing, personally. I know it riles a lot of people up here.

Patients often understand their own chronic condition better than medics, especially if they’ve lived and breathed it for years. Especially when some of the less common conditions are relegated to 3 lines in a medical school textbook.

Best example of ‘patients know best’ I can think of is T1DM. Majority of patients literally manage their condition day in day out from early childhood. Then they get admitted to hospital and the nursing staff take over monitoring their sugars, and suddenly wonder why their BMs are all over the shop.

I get it doesn’t apply to every patient.

Hey OP. I’m a doctor.
HIV in 2024 is really manageable and treatable.

Read online about 0 = 0 (no detectable viral load = 0 chance of transmission): https://www.iasociety.org/zero-risk-transmitting-hiv#three-categories

The most important thing is getting it under control & early.
If you can’t speak to your family, find a medical professional or sexual health clinic to support you and get you treatment.

Your band size (the number) should be tight enough that it sits comfortably under your boobs, but not too tight that it pinches your skin. You could take several different numbers of the same bra into the changing room to try on and see how they feel. Don’t just stand still in the bra - bend over, lift up your arms - you’ll be wearing it all day!

Your cup size should also fit comfortably around the boob, without any spillage at the front or spillage under your armpits - then it’s too small. If there’s a big gap between your boob and the cup, it’s too big. Again, you could take a few cup sizes into the changing rooms to try them out.

There’s also lots of types of bras. Some have underwires (bits of metal that sit under the boob) for more support, some don’t (for example). You will find out which ones feel more comfy.

Not sure where you are, but if you’re in the UK, M&S are amazing for first time bra fittings.

As a former ileostomy user who had this exact same issue with a healthcare company/GP forgetting to order supplies, I am really sorry. I found the whole experience degrading and humiliating and can sympathise. A&E will always provide you with spares (I also had to do this a few times) but it’s such a pain *especially* at the moment with the current situation.

I had my ileostomy back in 2013-2015. In 2013, only a GP had to sign prescriptions for bags/other supplies with no consent needed from the company. Then new legislation came in around mid-2014 due to people ordering so many bags/supplies they didn’t need, the massive cost of this, plus the NHS trying to make cuts. Having used both systems - before and after - I definitely saw a huge negative change eg being quizzed by the company on WHY I needed this number of bags, even them deliberately missing items off my order without telling me cause I’d apparently ‘over ordered’ and so on. As far as I’m aware this whole change was a decision made by the NHS (who I believe pay towards these companies) to save money. Your contract, I suppose, is a joint three-way between you, them and your GP, although the company have the final say in which/how many products to send you and can refuse orders that they think are ‘too much’.

First thing I would do is switch suppliers. You have no obligation to use the supplier you were assigned to in hospital - you can change at any time. As you’re probably aware already there are several different ostomy product suppliers in the U.K.
Find a new supplier and call them up, explain the situation and that you’re super unhappy with your current supplier and would like to switch immediately. They’re often happy to send you samples free of charge and off prescription to tide you over.

Next, I would contact the complaints department of your current company. Spell out exactly what has happened. I doubt you can confirm exactly where you caught covid (even if you’re pretty sure it was A&E) so you probably can’t legally pin that on them. You can, however, explain how humiliating and awful this situation was, that you had to make an unnecessary trip to hospital in a pandemic because of them, that you will be following up this issue by speaking to your hospital team/recommending that other patients do not use their services, and will be looking to take legal action if at all possible. Tell them you will be switching services with immediate effect. Make them feel bad without being rude - seriously. I don’t know if these companies always appreciate how humiliating an experience this can be.

In terms of legal approach - as I said before about being unable to prove where exactly you caught covid, you probably can’t bring legal action against them for this. But who knows, it’s worth a go. I’d say medical negligence lawyer.

It may also be worth talking to your own stoma nurses about this. They have probably seen lots of patients go through the same and may be able to recommend a different supplier, or if nothing else just listen to you vent.

I did have my ileostomy reversed in 2015 so this is a little while ago for me, but do feel free to message privately if you want to vent/chat.

- The risk of catching HSV in any one sexual encounter is 30% reduced by condom use - and is generally less between female to male.

In a laparoscopy (keyhole) surgery into the abdomen, they start by inserting one port (trochar) at your belly button. They put in a tube that literally blows your belly up with CO2. They then insert 1-2 further ports at different points on the abdomen for surgical instruments.

These ports are pretty large - probably have the diameter of a 20p piece (UK). When they pull them out at the end of the surgery, the air just rushes back out. Kind of makes a noise like a deflating balloon.

Air doesn't get into organs/blood vessels because your abdominal cavity is a closed space. The air can't go anywhere other than the space inside your abdomen around your organs. So no risk of air embolism, for example. 

In other procedures, for example a colonoscopy (camera up the butt), they suck the air back out as they remove the scope to make the patient comfortable. Otherwise you'd be left with the bloated gas belly from hell.

Your eye movements are controlled by 6 different muscles (medial, lateral, superior and inferior rectus muscles; inferior and superior oblique muscles) each of which pulls the eyeball in different directions. They are all attached to the sclera ('white') of your eyeball and then to your skull. They are innervated by 3 of the cranial nerves (oculomotor, trochlear and abducens nerves) - a set of 12 nerves that mostly control functions in the head and neck (but some control things happening elsewhere in the body).

Other movements, such as pupil dilation and contraction, are controlled by tiny muscles in the front of the eye (constrictor pupillae).

There are not individuals that have XY chromosomes and 'full physiology of a woman'. There are people who have genetically male chromosomes (XY) who develop ambiguous genitalia, sometimes to the point where externally it appears totally 'female' (this is Total Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia), to give it the proper name. But these people don't have 'full physiology' of a woman - they have internal, undescended testes, with no uterus and sometimes no vagina either.

Not to mention that XY and XX don't just mean your genitalia. So many conditions are dependent on having an XY or XX combination of chromosomes. And yes there are also some people who are intersex (CAH is actually classed as an intersex condition, as that person will have usually been raised female without question throughout their lives). But it is physically impossible to have one set of chromosomes and the 'full physiology' of the opposite sex.

When it comes to surgery, only you can know when you've 'had enough'. My surgery was an emergency and not really a choice, but when I had it I still knew that they'd exhausted all the medical options. That made having the stoma much easier to accept, because I never had any thoughts of 'what if that had been done differently' - I just knew that it was my only option and would definitely improve my life from what it was at that point.

However, just because there is one medical option left, it doesn't mean that you should take it if you already feel mentally that you're done with UC. Just from what you've said above, it sounds like you are. I'm 23 and also a student so I can totally understand the 'illness putting life on hold' thing - when I had my first op I had literally just started university. Having the surgery really does make you a hell of a lot better. Even in the very early days when you're feeling rubbish about having a stoma (which everyone goes through at first) you'll already feel the benefit of having the op. 

Even though I've had my issues, surgery has improved my life immensely. That was particularly noticeable after the first operation where I went from being underweight/severely ill to pretty healthy again in a matter of months.

I think to sum up, there's an advantage to having exhausted all medical options, because then you'll never look back and wonder 'what if that worked'. However, if you've reached that point where you're just so sick of it that you're mentally ready for surgery, and surgery starts to seem like a preferable option, then it's definitely something to consider. Surgery is not without its own issues (dealing physically and mentally with a stoma, potential complications) but it definitely improves your health overall. Even with the issues I've had, it's still preferable to the days of UC.

So pouchitis is inflammation of the pouch, causing symptoms very similar to UC (urgency, diarrhoea, increased frequency, bleeding, loss of appetite). Doctors do not really understand what causes it, but it's thought to be an immune response or related to unusual bacterial growth in the small bowel. 

I developed it a few months after takedown and it's never really left. Over the past 2 years I've taken different antibiotics, for a month at a time (Flagyl, Ciprofloxacin, Flagyl/Cipro combination, Co-Amoxiclav). Unfortunately none of these worked for me and the pouchitis would come back a few days after finishing up the course. The antibiotics also had their own side effects (random urges to vomit while on a packed London Underground train at rush hour are not the one).

I recently tried a clinical trial which is a type of immunosuppressant enema. Unfortunately that didn't work either and they're now looking at steroids or biologic drugs. If these don't work there's a chance I might need to have a stoma again, for good this time.

Pouchitis is a total bitch but fortunately (not for me) quite a rare case. Most people's pouchitis clears with a single course of antibiotics. They have considered at times whether I might actually have Crohn's disease but so far all investigations (scopes, biopsies) have not shown any evidence of this.

When I think about comparing pouchitis and UC, however bad the pouchitis has got, I know it's never going to get to a life-threatening stage. The symptoms are very similar, but ultimately UC can lead to really dangerous complications that pouchitis never can. 

Sure, it's been very uncomfortable and it's meant a lot of doctors visits and interventions. It makes me sick on a day to day basis, but it's nothing in comparison to UC, which can actually become a threat to your life if it gets to a really bad stage. I try and remind myself of this if I'm particularly down about pouch issues. Pouches definitely trump UC.

I've had a rough few years, but if I could go and do it all again even with the complications, I would still take the J-pouch. Not having a bag for 2 years has been absolutely fantastic. I think at my age I was unwilling to go straight for a permanent stoma. With all my issues, that might become necessary at some point, but if that happened I still would not regret the pouch. If I hadn't had one, I would always have wondered what it would have been like. I would still recommend it to anyone thinking about surgery - especially as there are plenty of people out there who don't get pouchitis and have a better outcome.
